prize_parts.citation: For the invention and realization of optical lattice clocks based on magic-wavelength trapping, opening a new regime of precision in frequency measurement.

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: a single-part B005 prize to Katori and Ye. Having read all eight round-1 statements and the chair's questions, I would put the criterion this way. A prize should go to a discovery or invention whose central claim is settled, whose credit can be written without a footnote, and which has changed what other physicists can do. B005 meets all three. The central step is one idea: choose the trapping wavelength so that the light shift cancels for the clock transition, and thousands of atoms can then be interrogated at once with Doppler and recoil effects suppressed. The realization took fractional uncertainty to about 1e-18, and that figure has been reproduced and improved on in several laboratories and with more than one species, so nothing depends on a single group's reading. On the chair's attribution question, my reading is that Katori is credited for the concept and the first lattice spectroscopy of strontium, and Ye for taking the clock to record accuracy and systematic control and for opening the many-body regime. I would word the citation as invention and realization, which describes the pair as co-inventor and realizer without claiming that Ye originated the magic-wavelength proposal. Six of eight files now reach the same configuration, but I rest the case on the science. The relevant test for the overlap with the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 prize for control of single quantum systems is whether the citation can be written so that it does not duplicate them, and it can: the magic-wavelength lattice is not part of either earlier citation.
statement.case_against: The reservations I hold are the overlap with the 2005 and 2012 prizes, the prospective status of the redefinition of the second, and the fact that other lattice-clock groups and ultrastable-laser developers sit outside the two names. I have narrowed the first by insisting on the tight citation above. The second I do not count as a maturity defect, because the science was settled once independent groups passed 1e-18, but I accept that colleagues weigh it differently. The third remains a real cost. I am working from memory on fine priority among Tokyo, Boulder, Paris and PTB, and I cannot settle it from the supplied text. If the committee found that another group had published the magic-wavelength proposal or first lattice spectroscopy before Katori, I would want the names revisited before the vote. The strongest case against my position is the one Mehlig and Danielsson put: that B014 reports a new phenomenon in nature, while a clock is an instrument. I take that seriously and do not think it is a trivial distinction. My answer is that the lattice clock is not only an instrument but a new regime for testing physics, and that I do not hold a prize for an invention to be lesser than one for a discovery, since the statutes name both.

responses.point: Mehlig asks whether a clock is a new discovery about nature, as moire quantum matter is, or an instrument achievement, and doubts that my opening ranking of B014 in seventh place settles the maturity question, since reproduction within eight years was unusually quick.
responses.response: The criticism of my seventh place for B014 is fair; I ranked it low in part on maturity, and rapid reproduction by many groups does count in its favour. I do not think the discovery versus instrument distinction decides this, though. The Nobel will is explicit that it covers discoveries and inventions, and a measurement that reaches 1e-18 does more than refine an old number: it makes gravitational redshift across millimetres, bounds on drifting constants and many-body effects in a clock observable at all. On Mehlig's own test, a prediction that could have failed, the lattice clock also qualifies, since the magic-wavelength condition was an explicit prediction that the light shift would cancel and the cancellation had to be confirmed. I remain more cautious than Mehlig about B014, because the pairing mechanism is open and the Cao question is unanswered, but I now regard it as a closer call than I did in my opening ballot.

responses.point: Eriksson argues that the prize is for the discovery of a phenomenon and not a finished explanation, so the open pairing mechanism does not weaken B014, that the correlated states are stable and widely reproduced, and that lattice clocks await a redefinition that the moire field does not need.
responses.response: I accept the first point. The discovery of correlated insulators and superconductivity at the magic angle is a result independent of the mechanism, and I withdraw any suggestion that the open mechanism alone makes the case premature. I would still say that the attribution is the harder difficulty for B014: the lead author of the 2018 experiments is outside the three seats, and the three-name list rests on a view of the 2011 model that Eriksson himself says is from recollection. On timing, I disagree that the SI redefinition is the issue. It is not a precondition for B005, and I would not delay on that basis. Eriksson is right that moire physics is moving fast. That is a reason to expect B014 to be recognised later, once the experimental credit is clearer, but not a reason to prefer it now over a case that is already settled.

responses.point: Danielsson says he is close to indifferent between B005 and B014 and asks whether Ye's contribution is co-invention or record-accuracy realization; he also wants the prize to go to nature surprising us.
responses.response: On Ye I would use the wording invention and realization and not claim co-invention. Katori's proposal and first strontium lattice work set the idea; Ye's group made the clock a precision instrument and tested it in the many-body regime, which is a separate achievement and not a minor one. I would not tilt the citation towards either, because the pair is complementary. I understand Danielsson's instinct for surprise but I would test it against the lattice clock itself: a larger statistical gain and a cancelled shift were a clever route, but the many-body behaviour of interrogated atoms and the redshift measurements over millimetres were not anticipated. If the committee is truly indifferent between B005 and B014, I would break the tie on the settled credit and the longer independent record.

responses.point: Olsson would keep the citation specific to the lattice clock, since the comb was recognised in 2005 and ultrastable cavity lasers are an enabling technology whose names are not on the ballot.
responses.response: I agree and I withdraw the grouping question from my round-1 file. My concern then was whether ultrastable-laser work should be treated as part of the clock. After reading Olsson and Lindroth I think it should be treated as enabling technology, since folding it in would add names beyond the three-person limit and blur the credit. I would still ask the committee to record that the cavity-stabilised laser sets the coherence the clock exploits, so that the citation language is not read as denying it. That is a matter for the citation text and the public background, not for the names.

responses.point: Pearce, the chair, asks that the claim of distinctness from earlier prizes be made explicitly and that the citation stay tied to the lattice clock invention and not to precision time in general.
responses.response: I agree and have changed my citation to reflect it. My round-1 wording spoke of a new regime of precision in frequency measurement, which could be read as a general claim. The revised citation names magic-wavelength trapping, which belongs to neither the 2005 nor the 2012 citation, and it stays with the lattice clock. I would not accept the bare wording without the magic-wavelength phrase, because that phrase is what carries the distinction from ion clocks and from the comb.

uncertainties: Fine priority among the Tokyo, Boulder, Paris and PTB efforts for the magic-wavelength proposal and the first lattice spectroscopy rests on my recollection; if a source check showed another group ahead of Katori, the names would need revisiting.
Whether the committee accepts a third prize in precision frequency metrology; I judge the magic-wavelength lattice distinct enough, and this is a judgment on which colleagues differ.
Whether the credit for B014 can be settled given the omission of Yuan Cao and the earlier band-structure theorists; this bears on whether B014 is a fair alternative and not on my choice.
How the committee wants to treat Zoller across B024 and B015, which I leave to colleagues closer to quantum information.
statement.conflict_note: No documented personal or institutional tie to Katori or Ye. For transparency I repeat that I spent a research stay in John Hall's laboratory in Boulder during my doctoral period; Hall is not a candidate, but the precision-laser community is adjacent to B005 and the committee should weigh my statement with that in mind. My other documented connections are to Sune Svanberg, Marcus Aldén, Lund colleagues (Rippe, Walther, Kinos), European quantum-memory collaborations, WACQT and Deep Light Vision; none involves a credited candidate. If B024 or B015 were pursued, Zoller's quantum-memory and quantum-optics community overlaps with my field, though I have no documented personal relationship. No change from round 1.
